issues.legal_issue: An execution process for delivery of possession ceases to be executable after the deadline specified in it.
material_facts: Processes for delivery of possession specified a date by which they had to be executed.
The attempt to execute them occurred after that date had passed.
issues.conclusion: The processes had ceased to be executable when the attempt was made.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXI, rule 24(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the process must be executed on or before the specified date. Rule 25 concerns delay in returning the process to court, whether or not it was executed, and does not permit execution after the specified date. The Court referred to Anand Lal Bera v. The Empress, Chelli Latchanna v. The Emperor, Nand Lal v. Emperor, and Kishori Lal v. Emperor.

predicates.execution_of_civil_possession_decree: A party sought to execute a civil decree for delivery of possession.
predicates.process_specified_execution_deadline: The process specified a date on or before which it had to be executed.
predicates.execution_attempt_occurred_after_deadlin: The attempted execution occurred after the date specified in the process.

issues.definition: When a possession-decree process specifies an execution deadline and execution is attempted after that deadline, the process is no longer executable.

issues.legal_issue: An entry on property is criminal trespass only when causing an offence, intimidation, insult, or annoyance is the aim of the entry, rather than merely a known natural consequence.
material_facts: The entrants entered land to carry out possession processes that had expired.
They had been armed with the processes and intended to execute them, and the courts considered it reasonable that they did not know the processes had ceased to be executable.
The entrants could have known that their entry would naturally annoy the persons in possession.
The circumstances supported execution of the processes, rather than annoyance, as the dominant purpose of the entry.
issues.conclusion: The entry was not shown to be criminal trespass, and the defence that the assembly had gathered to resist criminal trespass was rightly rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Section 441 of the Indian Penal Code requires the specified intent; knowledge that annoyance, intimidation, or insult will naturally result is relevant but is not by itself sufficient. The relevant purpose must be the aim of the entry, assessed in light of all circumstances, including whether another purpose was dominant. The Court relied on Bhagwant v. Kedari and approved Emperor v. D'Cunha, Nizamuddin v. Jinnat Hussain, Satish Chandra Modak v. The King, Bata Krishna Ghosh v. State, State v. Abdul Sakur, Queen Empress v. Rayapadaayachi, and Vullappa v. Bheema Rao. It disapproved the contrary approaches in Emperor v. Laxman Raghunath, Sellamuthu Servaigaran v. Pallumuthu Karuppan, and Kesar Singh v. Prem Ballabh.

rule.if: criminal_trespass_assessment and entry_on_another_persons_property and natural_annoyance_was_known and purpose_was_execution_not_annoyance

predicates.criminal_trespass_assessment: The court assessed whether an entry on property amounted to criminal trespass.
predicates.entry_on_another_persons_property: A person entered property occupied by someone else.
predicates.natural_annoyance_was_known: The entrant knew that annoyance to the occupant would naturally result from the entry.
predicates.purpose_was_execution_not_annoyance: The circumstances showed that carrying out an asserted possession process, rather than causing annoyance, was the dominant purpose of the entry.

issues.definition: If an entry is assessed for criminal trespass, annoyance is a known natural consequence, and execution rather than annoyance is its dominant purpose, the entry is not criminal trespass.

issues.legal_issue: An accused person's presence at a violent assembly, together with evidence connecting the person to it and the surrounding circumstances, can establish membership and the assembly's common object despite the absence of weapons recovered from that person's possession.
material_facts: The accused were found injured at the scene, away from the inhabited part of the village, after the mob dispersed.
Some accused were tenants facing dispossession, and the others were close relations of those tenants.
The Court accepted oral testimony of their participation and considered their presence and relationships inconsistent with their being mere curious onlookers.
Weapons were found in the field, but the evidence did not establish that they had been recovered from the accused persons' possession.
The mob had attacked the people seeking to take possession, and the Court found that the accused joined the assembly with the common object attributed to it.
issues.conclusion: The accused were members of the unlawful assembly with the common object found by the courts below, and their convictions on that basis were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated membership and common object as questions of fact, assessed on the accepted oral evidence and all surrounding circumstances. It found that the erroneous view that weapons had been recovered from the accused did not prevent the Court from independently accepting the evidence of participation. Sections 148 and 149 of the Indian Penal Code were applied to the assembly and offences committed in prosecution of its common object.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_unlawful_assembly_c: The proceeding is an appeal from convictions based on membership in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.credible_evidence_identifies_participati: Accepted oral evidence identifies the accused as participants in the assembly or its actions.
predicates.accused_found_injured_at_remote_scene: The accused were found injured at the scene, away from the inhabited part of the locality, after the assembly dispersed.
predicates.accused_connected_to_people_defending_po: The accused were tenants facing dispossession or close relations of those tenants.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_support_member: The circumstances made innocent presence as mere onlookers unlikely.

issues.definition: In an appeal from unlawful-assembly convictions, identified participation, presence at a remote scene, a connection to those defending possession, and circumstances inconsistent with innocent observation support a finding of membership with the proved common object.

issues.legal_issue: A finding that culpable homicide was committed in prosecution of an unlawful assembly's common object does not warrant substituting a murder conviction when the evidence does not establish murder.
material_facts: Two people died in the attack by members of the assembly.
The courts below found offences under the lesser culpable-homicide provision proved in prosecution of the assembly's common object.
The State appealed seeking convictions for murder, but the Court was not persuaded that murder had been proved.
issues.conclusion: The State's request for convictions for murder was rejected, and the convictions for culpable homicide not amounting to murder were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 302, 304 Part II, and 149 of the Indian Penal Code governed the State's request to replace the culpable-homicide findings with murder convictions and the basis for liability through the assembly. The Court concluded on the evidence that the lesser offence was proved but the murder charge was not; it cited no earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.state_appeal_seeking_murder_conviction: The State appeals seeking a murder conviction in place of a lesser culpable-homicide conviction.
predicates.deaths_occurred_in_assembly_attack: People died during an attack carried out by members of an assembly.
predicates.evidence_supports_culpable_homicide_but_: The evidence establishes culpable homicide but does not establish the more serious offence of murder.

issues.definition: When the State seeks a murder conviction for deaths in an assembly attack but the evidence proves only culpable homicide, the murder conviction is not substituted.

issues.legal_issue: Exceptional personal circumstances may justify appellate reduction of sentences for participants in an unlawful assembly, while sentences for other participants remain undisturbed.
material_facts: Six appellants were women, and no specific part in the occurrence had been attributed to them.
The circumstances supported the view that the women had not taken a leading part and had come to the field in connection with their families and fields.
Two male appellants were of advanced age at the time of review.
The remaining two male appellants did not have the same mitigating circumstances identified by the Court.
issues.conclusion: The sentences of the six women and the two elderly men were reduced to the imprisonment already undergone; the sentences of the other two men were not disturbed.
issues.legal_principle: Sentencing is ordinarily within the trial court's discretion, and an appellate court ordinarily has little reason to interfere with a sentence confirmed by the High Court. The Court nevertheless found interference justified by the particular circumstances of the women and the advanced age of two men. No earlier case was cited for this sentencing decision.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_reviewing_sentence and exceptional_personal_mitigation and (women_had_no_specific_role or offender_was_of_advanced_age)

predicates.criminal_appeal_reviewing_sentence: The proceeding is an appeal asking the court to review sentences imposed on convicted participants.
predicates.exceptional_personal_mitigation: The court finds particular personal circumstances that make the sentence unduly severe in the case.
predicates.women_had_no_specific_role: The convicted participants were women to whom no specific role was attributed, and the circumstances indicated they did not lead the occurrence.
predicates.offender_was_of_advanced_age: A convicted participant was of advanced age.

issues.definition: In a sentence-review appeal, exceptional personal mitigation that includes either the specified circumstances of women without a specific role or an offender's advanced age supports reducing the sentence to the time already served.
